method: Independent confirm pass: every listed component judged against the current LaTeX on the recursive input route (body entry, declared annex proof and any further on-route treatment cited in evidence) and against the held source at the cited locators; source items compared are the source's presentation of the same definition, theorem or example, its stated hypotheses, equivalent forms, cases and attached claims. Correctness was not assessed.

components.gap: Grinstead and Snell's counterpart Example 4.17 (p. 147), a test for a rare cancer with prior .001, P(+ | cancer) = .99 and P(- | no cancer) = .95, giving posterior .019 so that 98.1 percent of positive results are false positives, ends with an empirical claim: when a group of second-year medical students was asked this question, over half guessed a probability greater than .5. components.gap: Durrett (p. 214) introduces the nice-space theorem by recording that regular conditional distributions do not always exist, attributes the first example to Dieudonne (1948) with references to Doob (1953, p. 624) and Faden (1985), and explains the obstruction: for each disjoint sequence the countable additivity of P(X in . | G) holds only almost surely, so over many such sequences the exceptional sets may pile up. On the route only the bare nonexistence statement appears (def:p15-w02b-p15-008-limits, item 3); the attribution and the explanation of why a hypothesis on (S, S) is needed are not supplied.

components.basis: Spherical model and great-circle coordinates specified.

components.gap: Durrett's Example 4.1.8 (p. 210) is titled 'Borel's paradox' and states the paradox and its resolution: at first glance, for a uniform point on the globe, the longitude and the angle on the great circle should both be uniform; the longitude is, the angle is not, and the paradox evaporates once one sees that the angle is independent of the longitude, so its conditional law is its unconditional law, which is not uniform because there is more area near the equator than near the pole. The entry computes the coordinate laws and the nonuniform conditional law, but it neither names the example nor states the paradox and its resolution; the later phrase 'the Borel paradox' in bayes-factor-computation is not tied to this example.
